title: Syllabus
text:
Course description
Why do some population groups experience systematically worse health than others? This course examines the causes, measurement, and policy implications of health inequalities, with a particular focus on the role of public policy.
The conceptual part introduces definitions, measurement strategies, and theoretical explanations of health inequality, including behavioural, material, and psychosocial mechanisms. It also examines inequalities by socioeconomic position, gender, migration and ethnicity, geographic context, and across the life course.
The applied part focuses on the analysis of cross-national survey data, particularly the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) and the European Social Survey (ESS). Students learn to describe, compare, and explain health inequalities across social groups, countries, and over time.
Throughout the semester, students develop their own empirical research project. The course provides guidance on research design, data analysis, and interpretation, alongside opportunities for feedback and discussion. No methodological prerequisites are required, as the course introduces the necessary tools along the way.

The final grade consists of three components:

Written paper (65%): Empirical research paper based on ISSP or ESS data. The expected length is 2,500–3,000 words for individual papers and 3,500–4,000 words for group papers.
Presentation (25%): Presentation of preliminary findings from the empirical research paper.
Active participation (10%).

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text: We have learned how to measure a health inequality within one country. But is an inequality observed in Switzerland large or small? To answer that question, we need comparison. In this session, you will examine how health levels and health inequalities vary across countries and over time using the European Social Survey (ESS) and the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP).

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
About this session
This is a guided self-study session. There is no regular classroom meeting. Work through this page in the order presented and complete the exercises as you go.
The session builds directly on Session 2.
In Session 2, our basic question was:

How does health vary by education in Switzerland?

We now extend this in two directions:

Across countries: Is the educational health inequality observed in Switzerland larger or smaller than in other countries?
Across time: Has the magnitude of health inequality changed?

The empirical logic remains familiar:

Define → measure → compare → quantify → visualise → interpret

But comparison introduces an additional challenge:

Are we actually comparing the same thing?

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
3. Health inequality across countries
section: From a national estimate to a comparative question
text:
From a national estimate to a comparative question
Suppose we find that:

80% of highly educated respondents in Switzerland report good or very good health, compared with 70% among respondents with low education.

The absolute educational health inequality is:
\[
80\%-70\%=10 \text{ percentage points}
\]
Is 10 percentage points a large inequality?
By itself, the number does not tell us.
If comparable inequalities are only 2 or 3 percentage points in most other countries, Switzerland would appear relatively unequal.
If gaps of 15 or 20 percentage points are common elsewhere, the same Swiss estimate would appear comparatively small.
This illustrates one of the main purposes of comparative research:

Comparison provides a benchmark.
It allows us to ask whether an observed pattern is common, unusual, stable or changing.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
Three comparative questions
Comparative health-inequality research often asks three different questions.

1. Do countries differ in average health?
For example:

Is good self-rated health more common in Switzerland than in Germany?

This concerns population health levels.


2. Do countries differ in health inequality?
For example:

Is the educational gap in self-rated health larger in Switzerland than in Germany?

This concerns the distribution of health within countries.


3. Do health inequalities change over time?
For example:

Has the educational health gap in Switzerland become larger or smaller over the past decade?

This concerns change in inequality.
These questions should not be confused.






ImportantA healthy country is not necessarily an equal country



A country can have:

high average health and large health inequalities;
high average health and small health inequalities;
low average health and large health inequalities; or
low average health and small health inequalities.

Comparing average health and comparing health inequality are therefore different analytical tasks.

This is why comparative analysis should usually report:

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
Comparability is not automatic
Before comparing countries, we need to ask whether our measures mean approximately the same thing in each case.
Several problems can arise.

Question wording
The wording of a health question may differ between survey programmes.
Even small wording differences can affect responses.


Response categories
Two surveys may both measure self-rated health but offer different response categories.
A binary indicator such as “good health” may therefore not be constructed in exactly the same way.


Education
National education systems differ considerably.
International surveys therefore use harmonised classifications to make educational attainment more comparable across countries.
Even these harmonised measures are approximations.


Survey composition
Countries can differ in:

age structure;
education levels;
migration;
labour-market participation;
urbanisation; and
many other characteristics.

A raw difference between countries may therefore reflect differences in who was surveyed as well as differences in the relationship we are interested in.


Time
Comparisons across survey waves require additional care.
Question wording, coding, survey modes, participating countries and weighting procedures can change.






NoteThe practical rule



For this session, we will compare observations within the same survey programme wherever possible:

ESS with ESS;
ISSP with ISSP.

We will not treat ESS and ISSP estimates as if they formed one seamless time series.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
section: Part I: Comparing countries using the ESS
text:
Part I: Comparing countries using the ESS
We begin with the European Social Survey.
Our first comparative research question is:

How does educational inequality in self-rated health vary across European countries?

We will use ESS Round 11.
The basic strategy is:

Calculate health by education within each country → calculate the educational health gap within each country → compare those gaps

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
Step 1: Load the packages
Open RStudio and load the packages used in Session 2:
library(haven)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(countrycode)
If you have not installed them before, install them once:
install.packages(c(
  "haven",
  "dplyr",
  "ggplot2",
  "scales",
  "countrycode"
))

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
Step 2: Import ESS Round 11
The data are stored in the common project-level data folder.
From the Session 3 folder, import the dataset using:
ess11 <- read_dta("../../data/ESS11.dta")
Inspect the dimensions:
dim(ess11)
And examine the country variable:
table(ess11$cntry)
Unlike Session 2, we do not filter to Switzerland.
The country dimension is now central to our analysis.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
Step 3: Create readable country names
The ESS uses two-letter country codes.
For graphs, it is useful to create country names:
ess11 <- ess11 %>%
  mutate(
    country = countrycode(
      cntry,
      origin = "iso2c",
      destination = "country.name"
    )
  )
Check the result:
table(ess11$country, useNA = "ifany")

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
Step 4: Construct the health outcome
We again use self-rated health.
First inspect the original variable:
table(ess11$health, useNA = "ifany")
Create the binary indicator used in Session 2:
ess11 <- ess11 %>%
  mutate(
    health_good = case_when(
      health %in% c(1, 2) ~ 1,
      health %in% c(3, 4, 5) ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )
Check the new variable:
table(ess11$health_good, useNA = "ifany")

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
Step 5: Construct comparable education groups
We use the harmonised ESS education variable eisced.
Inspect it first:
table(ess11$eisced, useNA = "ifany")
For this exercise, we collapse the harmonised categories into three broad groups.
ess11 <- ess11 %>%
  mutate(
    education = case_when(
      eisced %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Low",
      eisced %in% c(3, 4, 5) ~ "Medium",
      eisced %in% c(6, 7) ~ "High",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )
Make the ordering explicit:
ess11 <- ess11 %>%
  mutate(
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")
    )
  )
Inspect the distribution:
table(ess11$education, useNA = "ifany")






NoteWhy simplify education?



The harmonised ESS education variable contains more detail than we need for this exercise.
Collapsing it into low, medium and high education makes the comparative pattern easier to see.
This is a substantive analytical choice rather than a property of the data. In independent research, you should always document how such groups were constructed.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
section: Step 6: Compare average health across countries
text:
Step 6: Compare average health across countries
Before analysing inequality, examine overall health levels.
Calculate the proportion reporting good or very good health in each country:
country_health <- ess11 %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(
    good_health = mean(health_good, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(health_good))
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(good_health))
Inspect the result:
country_health
Convert the estimates to percentages if you prefer:
country_health <- country_health %>%
  mutate(
    good_health_pct = good_health * 100
  )
Now visualise the result:
ggplot(
  country_health,
  aes(
    x = reorder(country, good_health),
    y = good_health
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent_format(),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Good or very good health",
    title = "Self-rated health across European countries",
    subtitle = "European Social Survey, Round 11"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







ImportantExercise 1: Compare health levels



Use the table and graph to answer:

Which countries report the highest levels of good health?
Which report the lowest?
Where is Switzerland located?
How large is the difference between the highest- and lowest-ranking countries?
Does this analysis tell us anything yet about health inequality within countries?



The answer to the final question is no.
So far, we have compared average health.
We have not yet compared how health is distributed between social groups.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
section: Step 7: Calculate health by education within countries
text:
Step 7: Calculate health by education within countries
We now calculate good health separately for the three educational groups within every country.
health_by_country_education <- ess11 %>%
  filter(!is.na(country), !is.na(education)) %>%
  group_by(country, education) %>%
  summarise(
    good_health = mean(health_good, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(health_good)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
Inspect the result:
health_by_country_education
For Switzerland alone:
health_by_country_education %>%
  filter(country == "Switzerland")
This should look familiar from Session 2.
The difference is that we have now repeated the same calculation for all ESS countries.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
section: Step 8: Visualise educational gradients across countries
text:
Step 8: Visualise educational gradients across countries
One way to inspect the result is to plot health by education for each country.
ggplot(
  health_by_country_education,
  aes(
    x = education,
    y = good_health,
    group = country
  )
) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent_format(),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Education",
    y = "Good or very good health",
    title = "Educational gradients in self-rated health",
    subtitle = "European Social Survey, Round 11"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
This graph may look crowded.
That is itself a useful lesson: a graph that contains all available data is not necessarily an effective graph.
We can instead select a smaller set of countries.
selected_countries <- c(
  "Switzerland",
  "Germany",
  "France",
  "United Kingdom",
  "Sweden",
  "Italy"
)
Then:
health_by_country_education %>%
  filter(country %in% selected_countries) %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = education,
      y = good_health,
      group = country,
      linetype = country
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent_format(),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Education",
    y = "Good or very good health",
    title = "Educational gradients in self-rated health",
    subtitle = "Selected ESS countries, Round 11",
    linetype = "Country"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()






ImportantExercise 2: Compare gradients



Look at the selected countries.

Is good health generally more common among respondents with higher education?
Is the gradient equally steep in every country?
Does Switzerland appear more or less unequal than the other countries?
Are there countries where overall health appears high but the educational gradient is nevertheless substantial?

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
section: Step 9: Calculate the absolute educational health gap
text:
Step 9: Calculate the absolute educational health gap
Graphs are useful, but we also want a numerical measure of inequality.
For each country, extract the health level of the low- and high-education groups.
One convenient approach is to reshape the data.
First create separate low- and high-education datasets:
health_low <- health_by_country_education %>%
  filter(education == "Low") %>%
  select(
    country,
    health_low = good_health
  )
health_high <- health_by_country_education %>%
  filter(education == "High") %>%
  select(
    country,
    health_high = good_health
  )
Combine them:
country_gaps <- health_low %>%
  inner_join(
    health_high,
    by = "country"
  )
Now calculate the absolute difference:
country_gaps <- country_gaps %>%
  mutate(
    absolute_gap = health_high - health_low
  )
Inspect the result:
country_gaps %>%
  arrange(desc(absolute_gap))
To express the difference in percentage points:
country_gaps <- country_gaps %>%
  mutate(
    absolute_gap_pp = absolute_gap * 100
  )
Now the interpretation is straightforward.
For example:

The proportion reporting good health is 12 percentage points higher among respondents with high education than among respondents with low education.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
Step 10: Visualise the absolute gaps
ggplot(
  country_gaps,
  aes(
    x = reorder(country, absolute_gap),
    y = absolute_gap
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent_format()
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Absolute health gap",
    title = "Educational inequality in self-rated health",
    subtitle = "High education minus low education, ESS Round 11"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
This graph now answers a different question from our first country graph.
The first graph showed:

Which countries have better average health?

This graph shows:

Which countries have larger educational health inequalities?







ImportantExercise 3: Health levels versus health inequality



Compare the two country rankings.

Are the countries with the best average health also the countries with the smallest educational health gaps?
Where does Switzerland rank on average health?
Where does Switzerland rank on health inequality?
What does this tell you about the distinction between population health and health inequality?

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
Step 11: Calculate relative inequalities
As in Session 2, we should not rely only on absolute differences.
Calculate the relative ratio:
country_gaps <- country_gaps %>%
  mutate(
    relative_ratio = health_high / health_low
  )
Inspect:
country_gaps %>%
  arrange(desc(relative_ratio))
A value of 1 indicates no relative difference.
A value of 1.20, for example, means that the prevalence of good health is 1.20 times as high in the high-education group as in the low-education group.
Now compare the country ranking based on:

absolute_gap; and
relative_ratio.

country_gaps %>%
  select(
    country,
    health_low,
    health_high,
    absolute_gap_pp,
    relative_ratio
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(absolute_gap_pp))






ImportantExercise 4: Does the measure matter?



Do countries receive exactly the same ranking when you use:

the absolute difference, and
the relative ratio?

If not, why might the rankings differ?
Which measure would you report in a research paper?


A strong answer is usually:

Both, together with the underlying group-specific health levels.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
section: Part II: Comparing health inequalities over time
text:
Part II: Comparing health inequalities over time
Cross-national comparison gives us one benchmark.
A second benchmark is time.
Suppose Switzerland has an educational health gap of 10 percentage points today.
Was the gap smaller in the past?
Larger?
Or broadly unchanged?
We can examine this by comparing different rounds of the same survey.
For the ESS, we use:

ESS Round 7; and
ESS Round 11.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
Step 12: Import ESS Round 7
ess7 <- read_dta("../../data/ESS7e02_3.dta")
Inspect the country variable:
table(ess7$cntry)
Construct readable country names:
ess7 <- ess7 %>%
  mutate(
    country = countrycode(
      cntry,
      origin = "iso2c",
      destination = "country.name"
    )
  )

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
Step 13: Harmonise the health variable
The aim is to construct the health outcome in the same way in both rounds.
ess7 <- ess7 %>%
  mutate(
    health_good = case_when(
      health %in% c(1, 2) ~ 1,
      health %in% c(3, 4, 5) ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )
Check the variable:
table(ess7$health_good, useNA = "ifany")
The coding is now identical to the indicator we constructed for ESS Round 11:

1 = good or very good health;
0 = fair, bad or very bad health.

This consistency is essential. If we changed the definition of the outcome between survey rounds, an apparent change over time could simply reflect a change in measurement.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
Step 14: Harmonise education
We also construct the education groups in exactly the same way as for ESS Round 11.
ess7 <- ess7 %>%
  mutate(
    education = case_when(
      eisced %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Low",
      eisced %in% c(3, 4, 5) ~ "Medium",
      eisced %in% c(6, 7) ~ "High",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")
    )
  )
Check the result:
table(ess7$education, useNA = "ifany")
We now have comparable measures of:

self-rated health × education

in both ESS rounds.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
Step 15: Compare Switzerland over time
We first return to Switzerland.
Calculate health by education in ESS Round 7:
ch7 <- ess7 %>%
  filter(
    country == "Switzerland",
    !is.na(education)
  ) %>%
  group_by(education) %>%
  summarise(
    good_health = mean(health_good, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(health_good)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
And in ESS Round 11:
ch11 <- ess11 %>%
  filter(
    country == "Switzerland",
    !is.na(education)
  ) %>%
  group_by(education) %>%
  summarise(
    good_health = mean(health_good, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(health_good)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
Add a survey-round indicator and combine the estimates:
ch7 <- ch7 %>%
  mutate(round = "ESS Round 7")

ch11 <- ch11 %>%
  mutate(round = "ESS Round 11")

ch_time <- bind_rows(ch7, ch11)
Inspect the result:
ch_time
Visualise the educational gradients:
ggplot(
  ch_time,
  aes(
    x = education,
    y = good_health,
    group = round,
    linetype = round
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent_format(),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Education",
    y = "Good or very good health",
    title = "Educational gradients in self-rated health in Switzerland",
    subtitle = "ESS Round 7 and ESS Round 11",
    linetype = "Survey round"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







ImportantExercise 5: Has the Swiss gradient changed?



Compare the two survey rounds.

Has self-rated health improved or deteriorated in each educational group?
Is the educational gradient visible in both rounds?
Does the gradient appear steeper or flatter in the later round?
Can you tell from the graph whether the absolute inequality has changed?
What additional calculation would you need?

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
section: Step 16: Quantify change in the health gap
text:
Step 16: Quantify change in the health gap
We can now calculate the absolute educational health gap separately for each survey round.
ch_gaps <- ch_time %>%
  filter(education %in% c("Low", "High")) %>%
  select(round, education, good_health) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = education,
    values_from = good_health
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    absolute_gap = High - Low,
    absolute_gap_pp = absolute_gap * 100,
    relative_ratio = High / Low
  )
Inspect the results:
ch_gaps
You can now compare both measures directly.
For the absolute measure:
ch_gaps %>%
  select(
    round,
    Low,
    High,
    absolute_gap_pp
  )
For the relative measure:
ch_gaps %>%
  select(
    round,
    Low,
    High,
    relative_ratio
  )






ImportantExercise 6: Has health inequality changed?



Based on your results:

Has the absolute educational health gap increased or decreased?
Has the relative educational health inequality increased or decreased?
Do the two measures lead to the same conclusion?
What happened to the underlying health levels of the low- and high-education groups?

Write a short interpretation of no more than three sentences.
Do not simply state that inequality “increased” or “decreased”. Specify the measure you are referring to.


This last point is important.
Instead of writing:

Health inequality increased.

a more precise statement would be:

The absolute difference in good self-rated health between respondents with high and low education increased from X to Y percentage points between the two ESS rounds.

The second statement tells the reader what was measured, between whom, and using which measure of inequality.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
section: Step 17: Extend the comparison across countries
text:
Step 17: Extend the comparison across countries
We can now combine the two dimensions of comparison:

How do educational health inequalities differ across countries, and how have they changed over time?

Rather than examining Switzerland alone, repeat the calculation for several countries that participated in both ESS rounds.
Start by calculating health by country and education in ESS Round 7:
health_ess7 <- ess7 %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(country),
    !is.na(education)
  ) %>%
  group_by(country, education) %>%
  summarise(
    good_health = mean(health_good, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(health_good)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(round = "ESS Round 7")
We already constructed the corresponding estimates for ESS Round 11:
health_ess11 <- health_by_country_education %>%
  mutate(round = "ESS Round 11")
Combine them:
health_over_time <- bind_rows(
  health_ess7,
  health_ess11
)
Select countries that occur in both rounds:
countries_both <- health_over_time %>%
  distinct(country, round) %>%
  count(country) %>%
  filter(n == 2) %>%
  pull(country)
Keep only these countries:
health_over_time <- health_over_time %>%
  filter(country %in% countries_both)






NoteWhy restrict the comparison?



The set of countries participating in the ESS is not identical in every round.
If we compared the average inequality across all countries in Round 7 with the average across all countries in Round 11, a difference could arise simply because the composition of countries changed.
Restricting the analysis to countries observed in both rounds makes the comparison more meaningful.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
section: Step 18: Calculate country gaps in both rounds
text:
Step 18: Calculate country gaps in both rounds
We now calculate the low–high education gap for every country and round.
country_gaps_time <- health_over_time %>%
  filter(education %in% c("Low", "High")) %>%
  select(
    country,
    round,
    education,
    good_health
  ) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = education,
    values_from = good_health
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    absolute_gap = High - Low,
    absolute_gap_pp = absolute_gap * 100,
    relative_ratio = High / Low
  )
Inspect the result:
country_gaps_time
We can now ask whether the educational health gap changed within each country.
country_gaps_time %>%
  select(
    country,
    round,
    absolute_gap_pp,
    relative_ratio
  ) %>%
  arrange(country, round)
For a smaller set of countries:
selected_countries <- c(
  "Switzerland",
  "Germany",
  "France",
  "Sweden"
)

country_gaps_time %>%
  filter(country %in% selected_countries)







ImportantExercise 7: Compare change across countries



Choose four countries that appear in both survey rounds.
For each country, compare the absolute educational health gap between ESS Round 7 and ESS Round 11.
Then answer:

Did inequality change in the same direction in all four countries?
Which country experienced the largest change?
Does the cross-national ranking remain stable over time?
What does this suggest about treating health inequality as a fixed characteristic of a country?

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
A note on survey weights
So far, we have concentrated on the analytical logic of comparison.
Survey estimates can also be affected by the survey design and by differences in respondents’ probability of being included in the sample. Surveys therefore provide weights that can be used for particular types of analysis.
The ESS documentation provides detailed guidance on which weights should be used for different purposes. The choice becomes especially important when we move from estimating patterns within one country to comparing or combining countries.






NoteFor this session



Our main objective is to understand the logic of cross-national and over-time comparison, rather than to develop a complete survey-weighting strategy.
For your empirical project, however, you should check the documentation for the survey and waves you use and justify your choice of weights. We will discuss this when developing your individual analyses.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
section: Part III: A second source of comparative evidence — the ISSP
text:
Part III: A second source of comparative evidence — the ISSP
The European Social Survey is not our only source of comparative data.
The International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) provides another opportunity to examine health and health inequality across countries and over time.
For this course, two datasets are particularly useful:

the ISSP Health and Health Care 2011 module; and
the ISSP Health and Health Care II 2021 module.

Because both modules focus explicitly on health, they contain measures that are not available in every ESS round.
Import the datasets:
issp11 <- read_dta("../../data/ZA5800_v3-0-0.dta")
issp21 <- read_dta("../../data/ZA8000_v2-0-0.dta")
Inspect them:
dim(issp11)
dim(issp21)
The coding differs between the two ISSP datasets. This means that variables must be inspected and harmonised carefully before making comparisons.






ImportantExercise 8: Inspect before you recode



Using names(), table() and attr(..., "labels"), identify in each ISSP dataset:

the country variable;
the self-rated health variable;
the education variable; and
the survey weight.

Do not assume that the variable names or missing-value codes are identical in 2011 and 2021.
Record your findings before proceeding.


This is an important part of empirical research.
A harmonised dataset does not eliminate the need to understand how its variables are constructed.

section: ESS and ISSP are complementary — not interchangeable

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
From description to explanation
At this point, we can describe substantial variation.
We can ask:

Which countries have better average health?
Which countries have larger educational health inequalities?
Are inequalities larger in absolute or relative terms?
Have inequalities changed over time?

But there is an important limit to what we have done.
Suppose we observe that educational health inequality is larger in Country A than in Country B.
That observation does not tell us why.
Possible explanations might involve:

differences in the composition of the population;
labour-market conditions;
income inequality;
healthcare institutions;
social policies;
health behaviours;
material living conditions;
psychosocial factors; or
other contextual differences.

Distinguishing these explanations requires a different analytical step.

Description tells us where inequalities exist. Explanation asks why they exist.

We will return to explanations in Session 5.
Before doing so, however, Session 4 introduces another important question: how people themselves perceive and explain health inequalities.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
Your empirical project
You now have the basic tools needed to formulate a genuinely comparative research question.
A useful structure is:

How does [health outcome] vary by [dimension of inequality] across [countries and/or time]?

Examples include:

How does educational inequality in self-rated health vary across European countries?


Did educational inequality in self-rated health change between two ESS rounds?


Is the gender gap in self-rated health similar across countries?


Does the association between subjective social position and health vary across countries?

For your own project, start thinking about four choices:

Health outcome: What aspect of health are you interested in?
Dimension of inequality: Between which groups or positions will you compare health?
Comparative dimension: Which countries and/or survey waves will you compare?
Measure: Will you use an absolute measure, a relative measure, or both?







ImportantPrepare your research question



Write down one possible comparative research question for your empirical project.
Then identify:

the dataset you would use;
your health outcome;
your dimension of inequality;
the countries and/or years you would compare; and
the measure of inequality you would report.

You do not need to commit to this question yet. The purpose is to translate a substantive interest into an empirical design.

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
text:
Recap
In Sessions 2 and 3, we have moved from the concept of health inequality to comparative empirical analysis.
You should now be able to distinguish between three questions:

How healthy is a population?


How unequally is health distributed within that population?


How do those inequalities vary across countries and over time?

Several principles are worth retaining:

Health levels and health inequalities are different quantities. A healthier population is not necessarily a more equal population.
Comparison provides a benchmark. A health gap becomes more informative when we can compare it across countries or over time.
The measure matters. Absolute and relative inequalities can develop differently.
Comparability must be examined. Similar variable labels do not necessarily imply identical measurement.
Description is not explanation. Cross-national variation can generate hypotheses about why inequalities differ, but it does not by itself establish the causes.

The empirical sequence so far has therefore been:

Observe → measure → compare

title: 3. Health inequality across countries
section: Next session: How do people perceive and explain health inequalities?
text:
Next session: How do people perceive and explain health inequalities?
So far, we as researchers have defined and measured health inequality.
In Session 4, we change perspective.
People also form their own judgements about why some groups are healthier than others. They may attribute health differences to, for example, individual choices and behaviours or to social and structural circumstances.
These explanations may matter for whether people regard health inequalities as a problem and whether they support policies intended to address them.
The next session therefore asks:

How do people perceive and explain health inequalities?

We will examine public perceptions and causal attributions of health inequality and consider how these relate to judgements about inequality and public policy.
This also introduces an important distinction that will remain with us throughout the course:

Observing an inequality, explaining its causes, judging whether it is unfair, and deciding what policy should do about it are four different questions.


Reading for Session 4
Baute (2025), Social Science & Medicine, 117946.
Before the session, consider:

If two social groups have different health outcomes, what information would you need before deciding why the difference exists — and whether it is unfair?

title: 2. How can we measure health inequality?
section: From a concept to a measure
text:
From a concept to a measure
In Session 1, we defined health inequality as:

Health inequality refers to systematic differences in health outcomes between individuals or social groups.

This definition is deliberately broad. Before we can study health inequality empirically, we have to make several choices.
Consider the following hypothetical result:

Among people with tertiary education, 90% report good or very good health. Among people with compulsory education, the corresponding figure is 75%.

There is clearly a difference between the two groups. But describing this as a health inequality requires us to specify three things.

Three building blocks of measuring health inequality
Health outcome × dimension of inequality × measure of inequality
For example:
Self-rated health × education × absolute difference

The first question is what aspect of health we want to measure. The second is between whom health is being compared. The third is how we quantify the difference.
These choices matter. Different measures can describe different aspects of the same distribution of health.

title: 2. How can we measure health inequality?
text:
2. Choosing a dimension of inequality
Next, we need to decide between whom health is being compared.
Health inequalities can be studied across many dimensions, including:

education;
income;
occupation or social class;
gender;
migration background or ethnicity;
age;
geographic location.

During the semester, we will examine several of these dimensions in detail.
For now, we focus on education. Education is particularly useful for learning how to measure socioeconomic health inequalities because it provides an ordered indicator of socioeconomic position.
A simple analysis might compare people with relatively low and high levels of education. A more complete analysis can examine whether health improves progressively as educational attainment increases.
This distinction leads us to two related ideas.

Health gaps and health gradients
A health gap compares particular groups, often two ends of a social distribution.
For example:

What is the difference in good self-rated health between people with low and high education?

A social gradient in health considers the entire social hierarchy.
Rather than simply comparing the lowest and highest groups, we ask whether health tends to improve progressively with socioeconomic position.






Note



A large part of health inequality research therefore concerns not only whether two groups differ, but also how health is distributed across the full socioeconomic hierarchy.

title: 2. How can we measure health inequality?
text:
3. Choosing a measure of inequality
Return to our hypothetical example:



Education
Good or very good health




Compulsory education
75%


Tertiary education
90%



How large is the inequality?
There is more than one reasonable answer.

Absolute inequality
An absolute difference expresses the difference in the original units of the outcome.
For our example:
\[
90\% - 75\% = 15 \text{ percentage points}
\]
The absolute health inequality is therefore 15 percentage points.
More generally, the rate difference (RD) between two groups can be written as:
\[
RD = y_1-y_2
\]
where \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are the health outcomes of the two groups being compared.


Relative inequality
A relative measure expresses the outcome of one group relative to the outcome of another.
Using the same example:
\[
\frac{90}{75}=1.20
\]
The prevalence of good health is therefore 1.20 times as high among the high-education group as among the low-education group.
The corresponding rate ratio (RR) is:
\[
RR=\frac{y_1}{y_2}
\]






WarningPercentage or percentage point?



These are not the same.
An increase from 75% to 90% is an increase of 15 percentage points.
Relative to the initial value of 75%, it is an increase of 20%.
Always state clearly which quantity you are reporting.

section: Absolute and relative inequality can tell different stories
text:
Absolute and relative inequality can tell different stories
Why do we need both measures? A thought experiment by Asada (2010) illustrates the problem.

Asada’s pill experiment
Imagine a population consisting of two equally sized groups — for example, men and women. Initially, their life expectancy differs:



Group
Life expectancy




Group A

Group B

Average

Now imagine that everyone takes one of two pills:

The red pill adds 25 years of life expectancy to both groups.
The blue pill doubles life expectancy in both groups.

Both pills produce exactly the same improvement in average population health: average life expectancy increases from 25 to 50 years.
But what happens to health inequality?






ImportantBefore continuing: make a prediction



How does health inequality change…

…with the red pill?
…with the blue pill?

Consider both the absolute difference and the relative ratio.

\]

But the relative ratio changes:
\[

\qquad \longrightarrow \qquad
\frac{55}{45} \approx 1.22
\]
According to the relative measure, inequality has decreased.


The blue pill: the same proportional improvement

But the relative ratio remains:
\[
\frac{30}{20} = 1.50

The experiment illustrates an important property of inequality measures: absolute measures are unchanged by equal absolute improvements, whereas relative measures are unchanged by equal proportional improvements (Asada 2010).

There is no purely mechanical answer to whether inequality has increased or decreased. The conclusion can depend on how inequality is measured.
For this reason, health inequality research should generally examine both absolute and relative measures, together with the underlying health levels of the groups being compared.

text:
Step 1: Prepare RStudio
Open RStudio and create a new R script.
At the top of the script, load the packages we need:
library(haven)
library(dplyr)

title: 2. How can we measure health inequality?
text:
Step 2: Import the ESS data

Download the ESS dataset provided for this session and save it in your working folder.
Then import it:
ess11 <- read_dta("../../data/ESS11.dta")
The object ess11 now contains the survey data.
You can inspect its basic structure:
dim(ess11)
names(ess11)
dim() tells you how many rows and columns the dataset contains. In survey data, a row usually represents one respondent and a column represents one variable.
You can also inspect the first few observations:
head(ess11)






TipDo not try to understand every variable



Large survey datasets can contain hundreds of variables. In applied research, you normally identify the variables relevant to your research question using the questionnaire and codebook, and then inspect those variables carefully.

title: 2. How can we measure health inequality?
text:
Step 3: Select Switzerland
The ESS contains respondents from several countries. The country identifier is cntry.
First inspect the countries included in the data:
table(ess11$cntry)
We now create a dataset containing only respondents from Switzerland:
ch <- ess11 %>%
  filter(cntry == "CH")
Check the number of observations:
nrow(ch)
From this point onwards, ch is our Swiss analytical dataset.






Note



The %>% symbol is called the pipe. It passes the result of one operation to the next operation. You can read
ess11 %>% filter(cntry == "CH")
roughly as:

“Take ess11, then keep observations for which the country is Switzerland.”
crumbs: 2. How can we measure health inequality?

title: 2. How can we measure health inequality?
text:
Step 4: Inspect self-rated health
The ESS variable health measures respondents’ general self-rated health.
Before transforming any variable, always inspect its coding.
table(ch$health, useNA = "ifany")
Because the dataset was imported using haven, the variable also contains value labels. You can inspect them using:
attr(ch$health, "labels")
The categories run from very good to very bad health.
For our first analysis, we create a binary outcome that equals 1 if a respondent reports good or very good health, and 0 otherwise.
ch <- ch %>%
  mutate(
    health_good = case_when(
      health %in% c(1, 2) ~ 1,
      health %in% c(3, 4, 5) ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )
Check the new variable:
table(ch$health_good, useNA = "ifany")
And calculate the proportion of Swiss respondents reporting good or very good health:
mean(ch$health_good, na.rm = TRUE)
Because health_good is coded 0/1, its mean is the proportion of respondents coded 1.
Multiplying by 100 gives a percentage:
mean(ch$health_good, na.rm = TRUE) * 100






ImportantCheck your understanding



What does the number you have just calculated mean?
Write one complete sentence reporting the result before continuing.
crumbs: 2. How can we measure health inequality?

title: 2. How can we measure health inequality?
text:
Step 5: Inspect education
The ESS provides a harmonised education variable called eisced.
Inspect it:
table(ch$eisced, useNA = "ifany")
attr(ch$eisced, "labels")

Before comparing health across educational groups, make sure you understand what the categories represent.
This is an important general principle:

Never analyse a survey variable merely because you know its variable name.
Always check its question wording, coding, missing values and substantive meaning first.

For the first exercise, we will create a simplified education measure.

ch <- ch %>%
  mutate(
    education = case_when(
      # INSERT FINAL CATEGORY CODING
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )
Once created, inspect it:
table(ch$education, useNA = "ifany")
crumbs: 2. How can we measure health inequality?

title: 2. How can we measure health inequality?
text:
Step 6: Calculate health by education
We can now calculate the proportion reporting good health separately for each educational group:
health_by_education <- ch %>%
  group_by(education) %>%
  summarise(
    good_health = mean(health_good, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(health_good))
  )
Display the result:
health_by_education
The output contains two important pieces of information:

good_health tells us the proportion reporting good or very good health;
n tells us how many respondents contribute to the estimate.

For easier interpretation, we can express the outcome as a percentage:
health_by_education <- health_by_education %>%
  mutate(good_health_pct = good_health * 100)

health_by_education







ImportantExercise 1: Describe the pattern



Look at the results and answer the following questions.

Which educational group reports the highest level of good health?
Which reports the lowest?
How large is the difference in percentage points?
Does the pattern suggest only a gap between the extremes, or also a broader educational gradient?
What can you conclude from these descriptive results — and what can you not conclude?



The last question is especially important. These results describe an association between education and health. They do not establish that education itself caused the observed differences.
crumbs: 2. How can we measure health inequality?

title: 2. How can we measure health inequality?
section: Step 7: Calculate an absolute health inequality
text:
Step 7: Calculate an absolute health inequality
Suppose the percentage reporting good health is \(y_H\) in the highest education group and \(y_L\) in the lowest education group.
The absolute difference is:
\[
RD=y_H-y_L
\]
You can calculate this directly from your results.

high <- health_by_education %>%
  filter(education == "High") %>%
  pull(good_health)

low <- health_by_education %>%
  filter(education == "Low") %>%
  pull(good_health)

rate_difference <- (high - low) * 100

rate_difference
Interpret the result in percentage points.
crumbs: 2. How can we measure health inequality?

title: 2. How can we measure health inequality?
section: Step 8: Calculate a relative health inequality
text:
Step 8: Calculate a relative health inequality
Using the same groups, calculate:
\[
RR=\frac{y_H}{y_L}
\]
In R:
rate_ratio <- high / low

rate_ratio
A rate ratio of 1 would indicate equal levels of good health in the two groups. A value above 1 indicates that good health is more common in the high-education group.






ImportantExercise 2: Absolute and relative inequality



Report your two results in words:

The absolute difference in good self-rated health between … is … percentage points.


The prevalence of good self-rated health is … times as high among … as among …

Which measure do you find easier to interpret? What information would be lost if you reported only one of them?
crumbs: 2. How can we measure health inequality?

title: 2. How can we measure health inequality?
text:
Step 9: Visualise the inequality
A graph often communicates a health inequality more effectively than a table.
ggplot(
  health_by_education,
  aes(x = education, y = good_health)
) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent_format(),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Education",
    y = "Good or very good health",
    title = "Self-rated health by education in Switzerland",
    subtitle = "European Social Survey"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
Look carefully at the graph.
Does it communicate the same pattern that you identified in the table?
What does the graph make easier to see? What information from the table is no longer visible?

section: A second dataset: can we reproduce the pattern?
text:
A second dataset: can we reproduce the pattern?
So far, we have measured educational health inequality using the ESS.
We now repeat the basic logic using a different survey: the ISSP 2021 Health and Health Care module.
This is useful for two reasons.
First, it familiarises you with a second dataset that you may use for your empirical project.
Second, it illustrates an important feature of empirical research: substantively similar concepts often have different variable names and coding schemes across datasets.
In ISSP 2021, the existing course workflow uses:

v51 for self-rated health;
EDULEVEL for education; and
WEIGHT_COM as the combined survey weight. :contentReferenceoaicite:2

Your task is therefore not simply to copy the ESS commands. You first need to understand how the corresponding ISSP variables are coded.

title: 2. How can we measure health inequality?
text:
Guided exercise: ISSP 2021
Download and import the ISSP 2021 dataset:
issp21 <- read_dta("../../data/ZA8000_v2-0-0.dta")
Then work through the following steps.






ImportantExercise 3: Reproduce the analysis with ISSP 2021




Identify the country variable and restrict the data to Switzerland.
Inspect the coding of v51.
Construct an indicator for good self-rated health.
Inspect EDULEVEL.
Construct substantively meaningful educational groups.
Calculate good self-rated health by education.
Calculate an absolute difference.
Calculate a relative ratio.
Produce a graph.
Compare the pattern with your ESS result.

Do the two surveys lead to broadly similar conclusions?
If the estimates differ, does that necessarily mean that one of them is wrong?


Do not worry if the numbers are not identical. Surveys can differ in fieldwork periods, sampling, question wording, coding, sample composition and other features.
The more important question at this stage is whether your substantive interpretation is supported by the evidence.

Beyond education and self-rated health
You now know the basic logic for measuring one form of health inequality.
But the same workflow can be applied to many other questions.
The existing ESS data, for example, also contain measures related to limitations in daily activities, depressive symptoms, alcohol consumption, income, urban/rural residence and social contact. :contentReferenceoaicite:3
The ISSP health modules contain additional health and healthcare variables and also provide a 10-point measure of respondents’ subjective position in the social hierarchy (TOPBOT). :contentReferenceoaicite:4

title: 2. How can we measure health inequality?
text:
Independent exercise
Choose one additional health-inequality question using either ESS or ISSP data for Switzerland.
For example:

Is poor mental health more common among people with lower socioeconomic position?

or:

Does self-rated health differ between urban and rural residents?

Your analysis should contain:

a clearly formulated descriptive research question;
one health outcome;
one dimension of inequality;
a description of how both variables are measured;
the health outcome for the relevant groups;
at least one measure of inequality;
one graph; and
a short interpretation of the result.







TipKeep the question descriptive



At this stage, formulate questions such as:

How does health vary by education?

rather than:

What is the effect of education on health?

The first asks about an observed health inequality. The second makes a causal claim and requires a different research design.

title: 2. How can we measure health inequality?
text:
What have we learned?
Measuring health inequality requires more than calculating a difference between two numbers.
Every analysis involves choices about:

what health outcome to study;
which dimension of inequality to examine;
how the relevant variables are operationalised;
whether inequality is measured in absolute or relative terms; and
whether we are interested in a gap between groups or a gradient across a social hierarchy.

The same population can appear more or less unequal depending on these choices. This is not necessarily a statistical problem: different measures capture different aspects of health inequality.
Good empirical analysis therefore makes these choices explicit and reports enough information for readers to understand what has been measured.

The basic empirical workflow
Research question → health outcome → dimension of inequality → variables → group-specific health levels → absolute and relative inequality → visualisation → interpretation

title: 2. How can we measure health inequality?
text:
Before Session 3
You should now be able to describe and measure a health inequality within Switzerland.
But this leaves an obvious question:

Is the health inequality we observe in Switzerland large or small?

To answer that, we need a comparison.
In Session 3, we will extend the same analytical workflow across countries and time. You will use the ESS and ISSP to examine how much health inequalities vary internationally and whether they have changed over time.

title: 1. What is health inequality?
text:
Why do some population groups experience systematically worse health than others?
This course examines how health inequalities are measured and explained, why they persist even in affluent countries such as Switzerland, and what public policy can — and cannot — do about them.

title: 1. What is health inequality?
text:
Bainvgnieu!1 Welcome!





The CHPE team.





I’m David Weisstanner, Assistant Professor of Health and Social Policy and co-director of the Center for Health, Policy and Economics (CHPE) at the University of Lucerne.
I am interested in how health and social policies shape people’s lives, why inequalities arise and persist, and how citizens respond to policy and social change.
University profile · Personal website · LinkedIn · Email



About you
To help me get to know the group and your backgrounds and interests, please complete this short questionnaire.




How this course will work
This course uses a modular teaching format. Sessions combine short inputs, examples and evidence, individual or group work, and discussion.
The course website is our common workspace. It contains the core material for each session and will often be used directly in class. Slides will be used selectively where they add value.
For each session, a print version of the website material will also be provided as a handout. You do not need to take notes on everything you see on screen — the core material will remain available on the website and in the handout.

title: 1. What is health inequality?
text:
Health inequalities are well known
People’s chances of living a long and healthy life differ substantially — not only between countries, but also between population groups within wealthy societies.

International examples…

20.7 years The difference in life expectancy between the highest- and lowest-life- expectancy groups in the “Eight Americas” study.

The classic “Eight Americas” study divided the US population into eight groups based on race, geography and socioeconomic characteristics. In 2001, life expectancy differed by 20.7 years between the groups at the extremes.






Figure 1: Life expectancy in the “Eight Americas”. Source: Murray et al. (2006).



Large differences can also occur within cities. In London, life expectancy varies substantially between neighbourhoods only a few kilometres apart.
Explore: Lives on the Line — life expectancy along the London Underground

Glasgow provides another well-known example of large spatial health inequalities.

 ▶ Watch: Danny Dorling on health inequality in Glasgow 




…and health inequalities in Switzerland
Switzerland has one of the highest average life expectancies in the world and a well-resourced healthcare system. Yet health is not equally distributed across the population.
The recent 2025 Obsan report on health inequalities in Switzerland documents systematic differences by education, income, gender, migration background and place of residence.
For example, in the 2022 Swiss Health Survey, 89% of people with tertiary education reported good or very good health, compared with 69% among people with compulsory education.






Figure 2: Education and self-rated health. Source: FOPH (2025, 3), based on Burla (2025).



Differences are also found for more objective outcomes. The recent Obsan findings show, for example, that men die twice as often from preventable causes as women, and individuals with lower education face an 81% higher risk of premature death from conditions that could have been prevented through healthcare or prevention (Burla 2025).






Figure 3: Deaths of 25- to 74-year-olds that could have been prevented through screening or effective treatment. Source: FOPH (2025, 10), based on Burla (2025).





Income, illness and healthcare use
Similar differences also show up directly in the healthcare system. A 2026 analysis by the University of Basel for Helsana linked health-insurance data with official income data.
It found that people with lower household incomes:

suffered more frequently from chronic diseases;
used more medical services and had longer hospital stays;
incurred higher healthcare costs; but
made less use of preventive services.

For example, depression was around three times as common in the lowest income category as in the highest. Chronic pain was also more than three times as common (Felder et al. 2026).
At the same time, lower-income groups were less likely to participate in colorectal-cancer screening — even where cantonal screening programmes were free of charge (Felder et al. 2026).



A crisis can amplify existing inequalities
The COVID-19 pandemic made these differences particularly visible.
According to the Federal Office of Public Health, socially disadvantaged groups in Switzerland were more likely to become seriously ill with COVID-19.
People with only compulsory education had an 80% higher risk of hospitalisation than people with tertiary education. The BAG also documents higher risks among migrant populations and people living in disadvantaged neighbourhoods (BAG 2024).


The geography of health inequality
Social disadvantage is not distributed randomly across Switzerland.
An interactive map based on the Swiss Neighbourhood Index of Socioeconomic Position shows substantial socioeconomic differences within cities and municipalities — sometimes across only a road, railway line or neighbourhood boundary.
Explore the interactive map of socioeconomic differences in Switzerland



Why does this matter for Swiss healthcare?

Different needs: some population groups experience substantially more illness and therefore require more healthcare.
Different patterns of access and use: treatment and prevention are not used equally across groups.
Planning and organisation: knowing where needs and barriers are concentrated matters for prevention, service delivery and resource allocation.

title: 1. What is health inequality?
section: Taking a step back: What is health inequality?
text:
Taking a step back: What is health inequality?
The examples above describe systematic differences in health between population groups.

Health inequality refers to systematic differences in health outcomes between individuals or social groups.

Examples include differences in:

life expectancy and mortality;
disease and disability;
self-rated health and wellbeing; and
access to and use of healthcare.

Importantly, health inequality is initially a descriptive concept. Observing a difference does not by itself tell us whether it is unfair, avoidable, or caused by social disadvantage.

(In)equality and (in)equity
These concepts are related, but they are not the same.

(In)equality describes observed differences, e.g. (un)equal treatment, resources or outcomes.
(In)equity introduces a normative judgement about what would constitute a fair distribution.

Health equity therefore goes beyond documenting inequality: it asks whether differences are unfair or unjust, and whether different groups may require different resources or support.






Figure 4: Equality and equity. Equal treatment does not necessarily produce equal opportunities or outcomes. Source: Burla (2025, 7).




This course focuses primarily on health inequality. We first ask who is healthier, how large the differences are, and what explains them. Whether a particular inequality is unfair is an additional normative question.

title: 1. What is health inequality?
text:
A roadmap for this course
The conceptual model below provides a useful framework for organising the different topics covered throughout the semester.
It distinguishes between the broader context, people’s social position, the intermediary factors through which social conditions may affect health, and the resulting distribution of health.
The model does not by itself explain why health inequalities arise. Instead, it helps structure the questions we will examine throughout the course and motivates the selection of topics in the syllabus.






Figure 5: Conceptual model of health inequality. Source: taken from Burla (2025, 8).




Reading the model
Context
Economic, political, legal and cultural conditions — including social, education and health policy — shape the distribution of resources and opportunities.
Social position
People occupy different positions in society. Important vertical dimensions include education, income, wealth and occupational position. Relevant horizontal dimensions include gender, migration background, age, sexual orientation and place of residence.
Intermediary factors
Social position affects exposure to resources and risks, including:

material living and working conditions;
psychosocial factors such as stress and social support;
health-related behaviour; and
access to, quality of and use of healthcare.

Health outcomes
These processes can result in systematic differences in mortality, morbidity, quality of life and wellbeing.

This model provides a roadmap for the course: over the semester, we will examine how context and social position are related to health, which mechanisms may connect them, where healthcare enters the picture, and what role public policy may play.

title: 1. What is health inequality?
text:
Session overview
The course follows the same broad logic as the conceptual model. Over the semester, we move from describing and measuring health inequalities to examining their distribution, explanations and policy implications.
We will cover:

Measurement and comparison — how large are health inequalities, and how do they vary across countries and over time?
Perceptions and explanations — how do people understand health inequalities, and which mechanisms may explain them?
Dimensions of inequality — socioeconomic position, gender, migration and ethnicity, intersectionality, the life course, and place.
Healthcare — how do access, affordability and healthcare use relate to health inequalities?
Public policy — which policies and institutions may reduce, reproduce or otherwise affect health inequalities?

See the full course syllabus

title: 1. What is health inequality?
text:
The empirical project
Alongside the substantive topics, you will develop your own empirical analysis of health inequality using international survey data.
The aim is to move from reading about health inequalities to analysing them yourself:

Research question → concepts → variables → comparison → analysis → interpretation → conclusion


The data
We will work primarily with two major cross-national survey programmes:

the European Social Survey (ESS); and
the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP).

Both provide individual-level survey data that allow us to examine health outcomes alongside socioeconomic and demographic characteristics, countries, time periods, healthcare experiences and attitudes.


How the project develops
The empirical work is integrated throughout the semester. At the beginning, you will work with guided exercises and predefined variables. As the course progresses, you will make increasingly independent choices about your research question, measures, comparisons and analysis.
The final paper brings these elements together in a small independent empirical study of health inequality.


The next two sessions: guided self-study
Sessions 2 and 3 are guided self-study sessions. There is no regular classroom meeting.
The course website provides the explanations, step-by-step instructions and ESS/ISSP exercises. Work through each session in the order presented.

Session 2: measuring health inequality and becoming familiar with the data
Session 3: comparing health inequalities across countries and over time

If anything is unclear, or you encounter problems with the data or code, please contact me.
